title: Grade 7 Science — Thu, May 28
description: Nutrition in Plants — Day 4 of 5: Special nutrition modes
subject: science

questions.question: Cuscuta (Amarbel) is yellow/orange and has no leaves. How does it survive?
options: It absorbs water from soil through deep roots
It is a parasite — uses haustoria to penetrate host stems and steal water and nutrients
It is a saprophyte on dead plants
questions.explanation: Cuscuta has no chlorophyll (can't photosynthesise), no real roots. It wraps around host plants and uses haustoria (penetrating structures) to steal nutrients.

questions.question: How does a pitcher plant (Nepenthes) trap insects?
options: It has a modified leaf shaped like a pitcher filled with digestive fluid; insects fall in and are digested
It uses thorns to spear insects
It moves quickly to catch insects
questions.explanation: The pitcher is a modified leaf. Insects are attracted by nectar and colour, slip into the pitcher, and are digested by enzymes in the fluid.

questions.question: Why does the Venus flytrap trap insects even though it does photosynthesis?
options: The soil it grows in is nitrogen-poor; it digests insects to supplement nitrogen for proteins
It uses insects for energy instead of sunlight
It traps insects to protect itself
questions.explanation: Insectivorous plants like Venus flytrap grow in waterlogged, nitrogen-poor soils. Trapping insects supplements their nitrogen intake for protein synthesis.

questions.question: Mushrooms, Rhizopus (bread mould), and Aspergillus are all:
options: Saprophytes — they break down dead organic matter
questions.explanation: These fungi are saprophytes (decomposers). They secrete enzymes onto dead material, break it down externally, and absorb the nutrients.

questions.question: Mistletoe grows on tree branches and steals water/minerals but still does photosynthesis. It is:
options: A hemi-parasite (partial parasite) — gets some nutrition from host but makes its own food too
questions.explanation: Mistletoe is a hemi-parasite: it has green leaves and photosynthesises (unlike total parasites like Cuscuta), but also steals water and minerals from its host.

questions.question: Why are saprophytes important in the ecosystem?
options: They eat pests that damage crops
They recycle nutrients by decomposing dead matter, returning minerals to the soil for plants
questions.explanation: Without saprophytes, dead matter would accumulate and nutrients would be locked away. Saprophytes release nutrients back into the soil — essential for the nutrient cycle.

questions.question: Cuscuta attacking a tomato crop is a problem for farmers because:
options: It takes over the host, weakening and killing tomato plants — reducing yield
questions.explanation: Cuscuta drains the host plant's nutrients and water. A heavily infested tomato plant is weakened, produces fewer fruits, and may die.

questions.question: Sundew (Drosera) is an insectivorous plant that catches insects using:
options: Sticky tentacles with glands that secrete digestive juices
questions.explanation: Sundew has tentacles tipped with sticky droplets. When an insect touches them, the tentacles curl around it and digestive enzymes dissolve it.

questions.question: Rafflesia (produces world's largest flower) is a total parasite because:
options: It has no roots, leaves, or stem of its own — it lives entirely inside the host plant's tissue
questions.explanation: Rafflesia is entirely parasitic on Tetrastigma vine roots. It has no photosynthetic structures — only the flower emerges. It is a total endoparasite.

questions.question: A plant scientist finds a plant with: no chlorophyll, thread-like body wrapping around a host, and small structures piercing the host stem. Identify the plant:
questions.explanation: Thread-like (no true stem/leaves), no chlorophyll, wraps around host, uses haustoria to penetrate — all describe Cuscuta perfectly.

questions.question: Lichens are a symbiotic relationship between algae and fungi. The algae provide _____ and fungi provide _____ to the partnership:
questions.explanation: In lichens: algae do photosynthesis to make food; fungi provide the structure, water retention, and minerals. Both benefit — this is mutualism.

questions.question: The pitcher fluid in pitcher plants is:
options: Digestive enzymes that break down trapped insects into absorbable nutrients
questions.explanation: The fluid contains digestive enzymes (and sometimes bacteria). These break down the soft parts of insects into nitrogen-rich compounds that the plant absorbs.

questions.question: How does Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules BENEFIT the plant?
options: By fixing atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia/nitrates that the plant can absorb for protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Rhizobium converts N₂ gas (unusable) into ammonia (NH₃) which becomes nitrates — the form plants can absorb and use to make amino acids and proteins.
options: By fixing atmospheric nitrogen into nitrates plants can use
By absorbing water for the plant

questions.question: Why can't saprophytes survive in sterile (no organic matter) soil?
options: They need sunlight which soil blocks
They absorb nutrients from dead organic matter — with no organic matter, they have no food source
questions.explanation: Saprophytes depend entirely on breaking down organic matter. Sterile soil has no dead organisms or their products — nothing for saprophytes to consume.

questions.question: A plant uses sunlight AND occasionally eats insects. This means it is:
questions.explanation: Insectivorous plants (Venus flytrap, pitcher plant) do photosynthesis (autotrophic) AND digest insects (heterotrophic). They are mixotrophs.
